Explain the role of neural reranking and retrieval techniques in modern search systems, and describe how they improve relevance by leveraging deep
Evaluate search engine performance using standard metrics and describe how to design a controlled experiment to test retrieval components.

courses.title: CSCI 99 — Undergraduate Cooperative Education Seminar
courses.subject: Computing Practice and Research
courses.description: An independent, catalog-aligned learning companion. It is not an official RIT course section or a replacement for the instructor's syllabus.
outcomes: Students will articulate the three core ethical responsibilities of computing professionals as defined by the ACM Code of Ethics.
Students will explain how responsible technical communication requires distinguishing claims from evidence and accurately reporting research results.
Students will identify the mandatory prerequisites and curricular requirements for registering for a Computer Science co-op program at RIT.

courses.title: Distributed Systems: Replication, Failures, and Raft Consensus
courses.subject: Distributed Systems
courses.description: Reason about partial failure and trace a client command through leader election, replicated logs, majority commitment, and recovery.
outcomes: By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to trace a client command through a three-node Raft cluster and identify the exact sequence of log replication and commit steps.
By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to explain how majority quorums and term-based voting prevent conflicting committed histories during network partitions.
By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to design a client retry strategy that avoids duplicate operations while maintaining system availability during partial failures.

courses.title: From a RISC-V Instruction to Pipeline Execution
courses.subject: Computer Architecture
courses.description: Trace an RV32I ADD instruction through encoding, the five-stage datapath, forwarding, stalls, control hazards, and performance.
outcomes: Decode the fields of an RV32I R-type instruction
Trace data and control through a five-stage pipeline
Explain forwarding, stalls, flushing, latency, and throughput

courses.title: Operating Systems: Processes, System Calls, and Virtual Memory
courses.subject: Operating Systems
courses.description: Trace how an operating system isolates processes, crosses the kernel boundary, schedules work, and maps virtual memory to physical resources.
outcomes: Students will accurately describe how user and kernel modes enforce process isolation through hardware privilege levels and system call traps.
Students will trace a single program operation through the OS lifecycle, identifying context switches, page table translations, and scheduler decisions at each stage.
Students will evaluate process creation and resource inheritance by applying POSIX fork semantics and copy-on-write virtual memory principles to real-world scenarios.

courses.title: Phishing Defense: Recognize, Verify, Report, and Recover
courses.subject: Cybersecurity and Digital Literacy
courses.description: Practice a complete phishing defense workflow covering manipulation signals, sender and destination inspection, independent verification, authentication protection, reporting, and incident response.
outcomes: Recognize consequential phishing warning signs
Verify identities and requests through independent channels
Report and respond to suspected compromise

courses.title: Analog Circuits: RC Dynamics and First-Order Filters
courses.subject: Electrical Engineering
courses.description: Build and analyze a first-order RC circuit from conservation laws through transient response, time constant, and low-pass behavior.
outcomes: Students will correctly assign consistent reference polarities and current directions to all circuit elements before writing equations.
Students will apply Kirchhoff’s current and voltage laws to derive and solve the governing equations for first-order RC circuits.
Students will calculate the RC time constant, predict charging/discharging transients, and verify steady-state behavior using energy and frequency-domain checks.

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics: Continuity, Pressure, and Bernoulli’s Equation
courses.subject: Fluid Mechanics
courses.description: Apply conservation of mass and energy to flow through changing area while stating exactly when Bernoulli’s equation is valid.
outcomes: Define a control volume and explain how mass conservation governs flow through it.
Calculate mass flow rate and apply the continuity equation to relate area, velocity, and density.
Apply Bernoulli's equation to a narrowing-pipe scenario while identifying valid assumptions and invalid applications.

courses.title: PID Control Systems: From Feedback Error to Practical Tuning
courses.subject: Controls and Mechatronics
courses.description: Build a complete PID control model from feedback error through term behavior, performance measurement, tuning, windup protection, filtering, and digital implementation.
outcomes: Explain proportional, integral, and derivative contributions
Interpret rise time, overshoot, settling, and steady-state error
Tune and implement a PID loop with practical safeguards

courses.title: Signals and Systems: Sampling, Convolution, and Fourier Reasoning
courses.subject: Signals and Systems
courses.description: Connect time-domain signals, LTI systems, convolution, frequency response, sampling, and aliasing in one coherent analysis.
outcomes: Define and distinguish continuous versus discrete signals by identifying their time-domain representation and mathematical properties.
Model linear time-invariant systems using impulse responses and convolution, explaining how system behavior emerges from input-output relationships.
Apply sampling theory to reconstruct bandlimited signals, identify aliasing artifacts, and trace a sinusoidal signal through a filter and sampler to verify frequency preservation.

courses.title: Solid Mechanics: Equilibrium, Stress, Strain, and Material Limits
courses.subject: Solid Mechanics
courses.description: Move from a free-body diagram to internal load, stress, strain, deformation, material limits, and an engineering design check.
outcomes: By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to construct accurate free-body diagrams and apply translational and rotational equilibrium to solve for unknown forces and moments
By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to calculate internal normal and shear stresses, relate them to normal strain and elastic modulus, and interpret stress-strain data
By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to perform a complete axial-member calculation with correct units, evaluate yielding and fracture limits, and apply safety factors
